title: Vacancy-Induced Topological Phase Transition via Valley Annihilation in an Anisotropic Honeycomb Lattice
authors: Anna Hassine, Amit Goft, Boris Rotstein, Eric Akkermans
abstract: A single missing atom can drive a topological phase transition in a lattice that is otherwise trivial for all values of its parameters. We demonstrate this in a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice with anisotropic nearest-neighbor hopping ratio $t'/t$. The pristine lattice is topologically trivial for all $t'/t$ by the Nielsen-Ninomiya fermion-doubling theorem: Dirac valleys appear in pairs whose topological charges cancel identically in any bulk invariant. A single vacancy breaks this cancelation, acting as an internal boundary with defect winding number $ν_3=\mp 1$ for $t'/t<2$. At $t'/t=2$, the two Dirac valleys merge and annihilate; the number of active pseudospinor degrees of freedom drops from $m=2$ to $m=1$, violating the condition $d+D+1=2m$ required for a non-trivial winding number. The winding number collapses to $ν_3=0$: a topological phase transition within a fixed symmetry class (BDI), driven entirely by a bulk Lifshitz transition and observable only through the vacancy. The defect zero mode crosses over from algebraic (${\sim}1/r$) to stronger spatial confinement, with its inverse participation ratio reaching a sharp minimum at criticality. Wavefront dislocations in the local density of states provide a direct, spatially resolved image of $ν_3$, accessible in graphene and in photonic and cold-atom analogs.
summary:
This paper demonstrates that a single vacancy can induce a topological phase transition in an anisotropic honeycomb lattice without requiring a bulk spectral gap closure. The transition occurs when Dirac valleys merge at $t'/t=2$, causing the defect's winding number ($
u_3$) to collapse from $\mp 1$ to $0$. This mechanism is diagnosed by observing sharp changes in zero-mode localization and topological invariants.
main_problem: The study investigates a topological phase transition driven by the annihilation of Dirac valleys caused by a single vacancy defect in an anisotropic honeycomb lattice.
main_result:
The system undergoes a topological phase transition at $t'/t=2$, where the defect winding number $
u_3$ collapses from $\mp 1$ to $0$, driven by the reduction in active pseudospinor degrees of freedom ($m: 2 	o 1$).
method:
The analysis uses tight-binding models, calculating topological invariants like the three-phase-space winding number ($
u_3$) and analyzing zero-mode profiles using diagnostics such as the Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR).
model_or_system: The model is a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice described by an anisotropic nearest-neighbor tight-binding Hamiltonian. The physics is analyzed in the context of symmetry class BDI, focusing on the impact of a single vacancy defect.
key_observables:
Topological winding number ($
u_3$), Active pseudospinor degrees of freedom ($m$), Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR), and wavefront dislocations in the local density of states (LDOS).
important_parameters: The anisotropic nearest-neighbor hopping ratio $t'/t$, with critical regimes analyzed at $t'/t < 2$, $t'/t = 2$, and $t'/t > 2$.
main_assumptions:
The analysis relies on the Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem for the pristine lattice and assumes the defect invariant $
u_3$ can be factorized into momentum and defect winding components.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the anisotropic honeycomb structure, the merging of Dirac valleys at $t'/t=2$, the evolution of zero-mode probability density (from algebraic to confined), and plots showing IPR minima and LDOS dislocation disappearance at criticality.
paper_structure:
The paper establishes the topological triviality of the pristine lattice due to valley pairing, then analyzes how a vacancy introduces $
u_3=\mp 1$ for $t'/t < 2$. The core argument focuses on the transition at $t'/t=2$, where valley merging causes $
u_3 	o 0$, marking a bulk Lifshitz-driven topological phase change.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed mechanism for realizing topological transitions purely through defect engineering, bypassing conventional gap closing criteria and linking it to fundamental changes in the system's symmetry constraints ($d+D+1=2m$).

figures.caption: Figure 1: Anisotropic honeycomb lattice with nearest-neighbor hopping ampli- tudes t (thin bonds) and t′ (thick bond), parametrised by angle α. A type-A vacancy (cross) removes one site and its three bonds.

Figure 2: Evolution of the Dirac points with hopping anisotropy t′/t. (a) t′/t < 2: two inequivalent Dirac points (valleys K and K′). (b) t′/t = 2: valleys merge at M0, yielding a semi-Dirac dispersion. (c) t′/t > 2: a spectral gap opens.

Figure 3: Zero-mode probability density for t′/t < 2 (periodic boundary condi- tions). (a) t′/t = 1: long-ranged, weight on sublattice B only. (b) t′/t = 1.5: mode spreads directionally but remains long-ranged and sublattice polarized.

Figure 4: Numerical vacancy zero-mode probability density for t′/t > 2 under periodic boundary conditions. (a) t′/t = 2.01: close to the critical point, the mode remains broadly distributed around the vacancy. (b) t′/t = 2.25: deeper in the gapped phase, the density becomes more strongly confined near the vacancy. Sublattice polarization persists in both panels.

Figure 5: Normalised IPR of the vacancy zero mode vs. t′/t for three system sizes (Nx ×Ny = 160×40, 200×50, 248×62; curves offset for clarity). Dashed line: t′/t = 2. The IPR minimum at criticality signals maximal delocalization (symbol gap closing); for t′/t > 2 the IPR rises sharply.
